UserGuide.generic.headerText: The title and description confirm where you are and the main task you can complete here.
UserGuide.generic.workspaceText: Choose a scope or item first, then inspect the details. Forms, lists, and tabs update to match your selection.
UserGuide.generic.actionText: Buttons create, save, or open more detail. Check your current selection and any on-screen guidance before submitting.
UserGuide.studentCourse.title: Course page
UserGuide.courses.title: My Courses
UserGuide.courses.step1.title: Choose a course from your course list
UserGuide.courses.step1.text: All courses currently available to you appear here. During the tour, a dashed safe-demo course is added so you can practice opening one without changing real data.
UserGuide.courses.step2.title: This is the tour's simulated course
UserGuide.courses.step2.text: The card shows its title, chapter count, and current progress just like a real course. The dashed border and Safe demo label mean nothing is saved.
UserGuide.courses.step3.title: Open the course to see machines and weekly content
UserGuide.courses.step3.text: Next opens this simulated course and continues the tour through its classroom machine, learning progress, and weekly tasks.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step1.title: The overview tells you what to work on now
UserGuide.studentCourse.step1.text: This area shows the course, current topic, and status. Check it first, then decide whether to enter a machine or review a weekly task.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step2.title: This bar is your course chapter progress
UserGuide.studentCourse.step2.text: It is not machine provisioning progress. It advances as you complete the learning content assigned by your teacher.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step3.title: Enter your classroom machine here
UserGuide.studentCourse.step3.text: In a real course, select the machine card to start and enter its terminal or console. The info button opens complete settings. The simulation never starts a machine.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step4.title: Weekly content is collected here
UserGuide.studentCourse.step4.text: Each row is one week and shows its date, check count, and completion state. Each week has one overall completion checkbox.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step5.title: Open a week to see feedback and its machine
UserGuide.studentCourse.step5.text: Next opens the simulated first week and demonstrates check feedback, the machine selected for that week, and course materials.
UserGuide.courseWeek.title: Weekly Course Content
UserGuide.courseWeek.step1.title: Confirm the course, week, and date in the header
UserGuide.courseWeek.step1.text: First make sure you are in the correct course and week. Use Back to Course to return to the complete list of weeks.
UserGuide.courseWeek.step2.title: Review the latest feedback for each check here
UserGuide.courseWeek.step2.text: You can see status, score, and comments shared by your teacher or AI. Opening this page only shows results; it does not run the check again.
UserGuide.courseWeek.step3.title: This is the machine selected for the week
UserGuide.courseWeek.step3.text: In a real course, open a published service URL or go to the machine and console for full status. The simulation never creates or starts a machine.
UserGuide.courseWeek.step4.title: Weekly materials are collected here
UserGuide.courseWeek.step4.text: A material opens in a new tab. The simulated file only demonstrates its location and downloads nothing.
UserGuide.studentHome.title: Home
UserGuide.studentHome.step1.title: Start with your ongoing courses
UserGuide.studentHome.step1.text: Courses appear here for their entire duration, not just on class day. Green means the class is currently in session; you can still click into other courses to use machines, check assignments, or practice after class.
UserGuide.studentHome.step2.title: Quick practice doesn't need manual review
UserGuide.studentHome.step2.text: When you need to quickly test a command or do some lightweight practice, choose a template and fill in a container name and password — the system approves it automatically and starts creating it.
UserGuide.studentHome.step3.title: After-class practice or independent research
UserGuide.studentHome.step3.text: When it's not time for class, you can pick up where you left off in your last course from here; independent research takes you to a resource request instead.
UserGuide.studentHome.step4.title: This is the class you're taking right now
UserGuide.studentHome.step4.text: The course name, class time, and "In session" status are all shown on this card. Check here first on the home page to know which class to join today.
UserGuide.studentHome.step5.title: This is your chapter completion progress
UserGuide.studentHome.step5.text: The progress bar shows how much of the current chapter you've completed — it is not the machine creation progress. This number moves forward as you finish tasks.
UserGuide.studentHome.step6.title: Click directly on the classroom machine you want to use
UserGuide.studentHome.step6.text: Machines assigned by your teacher are listed directly here. Click anywhere on a machine card to start and enter it; the info button on the right takes you to "My Resources" to view full settings.
UserGuide.studentHome.step7.title: Check whether the environment is ready first
UserGuide.studentHome.step7.text: "Environment ready" means you can get started. The IP is the connection address; "Usable until" is when this classroom machine expires.
UserGuide.studentHome.step8.title: Check completion counts here
UserGuide.studentHome.step8.text: Each task has its own completion checkbox. Tick it when you're done, and untick it any time if it isn't finished yet.
UserGuide.studentHome.step9.title: These are the grading items your teacher has assigned to AI
UserGuide.studentHome.step9.text: Only checks your teacher has approved are shown here. This only records your completion status; it doesn't start an AI check or judge whether you're right or wrong.
UserGuide.myRequests.title: My Requests
UserGuide.myRequests.step1.title: This is the actual resource request form
UserGuide.myRequests.step1.text: The guide has taken you directly into the form. Use it for a project or independent-research VM/container; classroom machines assigned by a teacher do not need another request.
UserGuide.myRequests.step2.title: Ask AI when you are unsure what to enter
UserGuide.myRequests.step2.text: Open the AI assistant at the bottom-right and describe your goal, such as “I need to host a Python website for two weeks.” It will ask for missing details, recommend a suitable size, and help fill this form. You can still edit everything before submitting.
UserGuide.myRequests.step3.title: Name the resource, then choose an OS
UserGuide.myRequests.step3.text: The name helps you identify it later. Choosing an image or environment template determines whether a VM or container is created and loads its recommended base specification.
UserGuide.myRequests.step4.title: Match the hardware to the workload
UserGuide.myRequests.step4.text: More CPU, memory, and disk use more quota. The recommended values suit most sites and exercises; choose a VM or GPU only when a GUI, Windows, or accelerated compute is needed.
UserGuide.myRequests.step5.title: Set when you actually need it
UserGuide.myRequests.step5.text: Use Immediate when starting now or schedule exact dates for a course or planned task. An end date lets the system reserve and release resources correctly.
UserGuide.myRequests.step6.title: Explain the purpose for the reviewer
UserGuide.myRequests.step6.text: Briefly state the project, course, or service and why it needs these specifications. The AI assistant can also draft an editable reason from your previous choices.
UserGuide.myRequests.step7.title: The summary updates as you fill the form
UserGuide.myRequests.step7.text: Before submitting, verify the type, name, operating system, hardware, and period. Every change is reflected in this summary card.
UserGuide.myRequests.step8.title: Submit only after everything looks right
UserGuide.myRequests.step8.text: After submitting, you return to My Requests to track review and provisioning. Only this button creates the request; the guide itself never submits data.
UserGuide.myResources.title: My Resources
UserGuide.myResources.step1.title: These numbers are your usage quota
UserGuide.myResources.step1.text: The number on the left is your current usage; the one on the right is your available limit. For example, "2 / 4 units" means you've used 2 and can have up to 4. When you're close to the limit, you'll need to release a resource first.
UserGuide.myResources.step2.title: Each card represents one machine
UserGuide.myResources.step2.text: The IP is the machine's connection address; the status in the top-right corner shows whether it's usable. Click the machine name to see its full details.
UserGuide.myResources.step3.title: Use this button to enter the machine
UserGuide.myResources.step3.text: When the machine shows "Running", you can click "Terminal" or "Console" to start working. The three-dot button next to it lets you power on, shut down, or restart.
UserGuide.firewall.title: Firewall
UserGuide.firewall.step1.title: Step 1: Point at a dot on the source machine's edge
UserGuide.firewall.step1.text: First decide which machine the connection starts from. Hover over the source machine and connection dots appear on all four sides. You can start dragging from any of them; the line automatically leaves from the side closest to the destination.
UserGuide.firewall.dragMove.title: Step 2: Hold the dot and keep dragging
UserGuide.firewall.dragMove.text: Press and hold the left mouse button on the dot. Keep holding it while moving the pointer toward the destination machine. The animation demonstrates the full movement.
UserGuide.firewall.dragTarget.title: Step 3: Release over a dot on the destination machine
UserGuide.firewall.dragTarget.text: Move the pointer onto the center of a dot on the destination machine's edge and then release. A successful drop opens the connection settings so you can choose an allowed port. If nothing opens, try again and align with the dot more precisely.
UserGuide.firewall.step2.title: Or complete it with Add Connection
UserGuide.firewall.step2.text: If dragging is inconvenient, click "Add Connection" and choose the source, destination, and allowed port. There's no need to add one without a clear requirement.
UserGuide.firewall.step3.title: Lines represent currently allowed connections
UserGuide.firewall.step3.text: Each box represents a VM, and the lines between boxes represent allowed traffic. Click a VM to view its rules; the number on a line is the open port.
UserGuide.firewall.step4.title: These buttons only change how you view it
UserGuide.firewall.step4.text: "Auto-arrange" tidies up positions; "Connection labels" shows or hides ports; "Map" toggles the thumbnail in the bottom-right corner. None of these modify any firewall rules.
UserGuide.reverseProxy.title: Reverse Proxy
UserGuide.reverseProxy.step1.title: Turn a VM service into an easy-to-remember URL
UserGuide.reverseProxy.step1.text: Once the website or API inside your VM is running, click "Add Domain" and choose the VM, the service port, and the URL. The system handles the outbound routing for you.
UserGuide.reverseProxy.step2.title: Each row is one public URL
UserGuide.reverseProxy.step2.text: The VM number is the target machine's ID, and the port is the one the service inside the VM listens on; the HTTPS label indicates a secure connection. Click "Open" to test the URL directly.
UserGuide.domain.title: Domain Management
UserGuide.domain.step1.title: Set up Cloudflare the first time you use this
UserGuide.domain.step1.text: Click "Connection Settings" and enter your Account ID and API Token. "Test Connection" only verifies that the settings are valid — it does not modify DNS.
UserGuide.domain.step2.title: This shows whether the connection is working
UserGuide.domain.step2.text: "Connected" means the platform can manage DNS; the last verified time helps you judge whether the credentials are still valid. Domains can't be loaded while disconnected.
UserGuide.domain.step3.title: The Zones number is how many domains you can manage
UserGuide.domain.step3.text: For example, "Zones (3)" means there are 3 domains available in the account. Click a domain on the left first, and its DNS records will appear on the right.
UserGuide.domain.step4.title: Search or add DNS records here
UserGuide.domain.step4.text: Use the search box to find existing records; "Add Record" creates a mapping between a name and an IP/service. If you're unsure about the record type, don't modify a production domain directly.
UserGuide.aiApi.title: AI API
UserGuide.aiApi.step1.title: These four numbers are your request and key counts
UserGuide.aiApi.step1.text: "Active keys" is the number of keys that can currently call the API; "Expired keys" can no longer be used; "Approved requests" doesn't necessarily equal the number of currently valid keys.
UserGuide.aiApi.step2.title: Three tabs plus the "Add Key" dialog
UserGuide.aiApi.step2.text: Click "+ Add Key" on the API Keys tab to submit a request; once approved, the key appears below. Track the review in Request Records and check actual consumption in My Usage. Next, we'll walk through each step.
UserGuide.aiApi.step3.title: "+ Add Key": request a new API key
UserGuide.aiApi.step3.text: Clicking this button opens the request dialog, telling the reviewer "which project needs AI and for how long". You won't get a key immediately after submitting — you'll need to wait for approval.
UserGuide.aiApi.step4.title: The key name is just for your own reference
UserGuide.aiApi.step4.text: We recommend entering your course or project name, such as "Capstone Project Chatbot". It is not the API key itself, and you can change it later.
UserGuide.aiApi.step5.title: The purpose of your request is shown to the reviewer
UserGuide.aiApi.step5.text: Write at least 10 characters, clearly describing the course, project, and the feature you plan to integrate — this is far easier for the reviewer to understand than just writing "test".
UserGuide.aiApi.step6.title: The validity period determines how long the key can be used
UserGuide.aiApi.step6.text: Choose a few days for short-term assignments, or a longer period for long-term projects. Once it expires, the API key stops working, but your request record isn't deleted.
UserGuide.aiApi.step7.title: Submit only once all information is complete
UserGuide.aiApi.step7.text: When the button lights up, your input meets the basic requirements. The dialog closes after submitting; check "Request Records" for progress — once approved, your key appears in "API Keys".
UserGuide.aiApi.step8.title: API Keys: Get the connection info your program needs
UserGuide.aiApi.step8.text: A key only appears on this page after your request is approved. Your program typically needs two values: the Base URL and the API Key. Treat the API Key like a password — don't paste it into assignments or public repositories.
UserGuide.aiApi.step9.title: Each card represents one issued key
UserGuide.aiApi.step9.text: The status shows whether the key can be used, along with its creation and expiration times. If the screen shows "No keys yet", it means no request has been approved yet.
UserGuide.aiApi.step10.title: The difference between show, copy, refresh, and delete
UserGuide.aiApi.step10.text: Copy is for pasting into your own program; Refresh generates a new key and invalidates the old one; Delete can't be undone, and any program currently using that key will fail to connect.
UserGuide.aiApi.step11.title: Request Records: Check where the review stands
UserGuide.aiApi.step11.text: Every AI API request you've submitted is kept on this page. It only shows the request and its review outcome — it's not where you retrieve keys.
UserGuide.aiApi.step12.title: Status and notes tell you what to do next
UserGuide.aiApi.step12.text: "Pending review" means it hasn't been processed yet; once "Approved", go to API Keys to retrieve it; if "Rejected", check the review notes and adjust your request based on the reason given.
UserGuide.aiApi.step13.title: My Usage: See how much AI your program has actually used
UserGuide.aiApi.step13.text: This page shows usage trends and token consumption — it doesn't display or modify your API Key. If usage spikes suddenly, check whether your program is calling the API repeatedly by mistake.
UserGuide.aiApi.step14.title: First choose the date range to analyze
UserGuide.aiApi.step14.text: The 7, 30, and 90-day options only change the report range — they don't limit your key's validity period. The dates on the right show the actual start and end dates currently covered by the report.
UserGuide.aiApi.step15.title: Unified usage: both routes combined into one total
UserGuide.aiApi.step15.text: Total calls sums the AI model route and the AI system route. Input Tokens is the text sent to the model, Output Tokens is what it returned, and you can inspect usage per model further below.
UserGuide.aiApi.step16.title: Call details: audit every single call
UserGuide.aiApi.step16.text: Each row lists the time, call type, model, tokens, and success/failure status. Failed calls include the error message to help you debug.
UserGuide.myResources.request.title: Request a resource here when the list is empty
UserGuide.myResources.request.text: Resource Request opens the full application form. Fill it yourself or ask the AI assistant in the bottom-right to organize your needs and help complete it.
UserGuide.myResources.row.title: Read a machine's status at a glance
UserGuide.myResources.row.text: The name, system, runtime state, private IP, expiry, and node are shown in one row. If you have no resources, this is safe sample data and creates nothing.
UserGuide.myResources.console.title: Connect to the machine here
UserGuide.myResources.console.text: LXC opens a terminal and a VM opens a graphical console. The machine must be running. The guide never makes a real connection.
UserGuide.myResources.power.title: More actions contains power and management tools
UserGuide.myResources.power.text: Start, shut down, reboot, or reset the machine here. With permission, you can also convert it to a template or delete it; risky actions still require confirmation.
UserGuide.myResources.detail.title: Open the machine name to see every setting
UserGuide.myResources.detail.text: Next, the guide enters this machine's detail page. If the account has no resources, it opens a read-only simulated detail page.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.title: Machine details and settings
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step1.title: Six tabs organize every machine function
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step1.text: The guide will open Overview, Monitoring, Specifications, Snapshots, Audit Logs, and Advanced Settings in sequence.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step2.title: Overview: status and access information
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step2.text: Find power state, IP, usage, expiry, and SSH or service links here. This is normally the first place to check.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step3.title: Monitoring: live and historical usage
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step3.text: Review CPU, memory, disk, and network traffic, then change the time range to decide whether resources need adjustment.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step4.title: Specifications: CPU, memory, and disk
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step4.text: Use the controls to request a specification change. Regular users submit for review; administrators can apply changes directly.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step5.title: Snapshots: recoverable points in time
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step5.text: Create a snapshot before upgrades or experiments and restore it when needed. The guide never creates, restores, or deletes one.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step6.title: Audit logs: who changed what and when
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step6.text: Power, specification, and settings changes appear here for troubleshooting and accountability.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step7.title: Advanced Settings: complete machine management
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step7.text: Lifecycle, firewall, boot order, credentials, metadata, and sharing are explained next.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step8.title: Lifecycle and expiry
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step8.text: Manage expiry, automatic shutdown, and pending schedules. These settings affect when the machine stops or is reclaimed.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step9.title: Per-machine firewall
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step9.text: Manage allowed inbound and outbound traffic. Check source, protocol, and port carefully before saving.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step10.title: Boot devices and order
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step10.text: Prioritize disk, network, and ISO boot devices, and mount or unmount installation media.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step11.title: Passwords and SSH keys
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step11.text: Reset credentials, update the platform key, or add a personal SSH public key. Sensitive values only appear when needed.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step13.title: Sharing and ownership
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step13.text: Grant access or transfer ownership. Verify the recipient and whether you retain access before transferring.
UserGuide.firewall.endpoints.title: The form first asks what you want to do
UserGuide.firewall.endpoints.text: The guide has opened the real Add Connection dialog. Pick an intent first: let a machine reach the internet, expose a service, connect two machines, or write a rule yourself. Then choose the machine and allowed ports; the direction follows the intent.
UserGuide.firewall.dialogActions.title: Create only after reviewing the rule
UserGuide.firewall.dialogActions.text: Check direction, protocol, and port before submitting. The guide demonstrates the form and never submits it.
UserGuide.firewall.map.title: Return to the topology to verify the result
UserGuide.firewall.map.text: Each line is an allowed connection and its label shows the port. Select a machine to inspect its own rules.
UserGuide.reverseProxy.domain.title: Compose the public URL
UserGuide.reverseProxy.domain.text: Enter a hostname prefix and select a connected domain suffix to form the final address.
UserGuide.reverseProxy.port.title: Choose the service's internal port
UserGuide.reverseProxy.port.text: Pick a common port or switch to a custom one. When HTTPS is enabled, the system handles the public certificate.
UserGuide.reverseProxy.actions.title: Create only after the preview is correct
UserGuide.reverseProxy.actions.text: Verify the VM, URL, and port preview before creating. The guide never submits or changes a rule.
UserGuide.reverseProxy.list.title: Created URLs return to this list
UserGuide.reverseProxy.list.text: Open the public URL directly, or edit and delete it on the right. Deletion requires confirmation.
UserGuide.domain.configForm.title: Connection Settings opens the complete form
UserGuide.domain.configForm.text: Enter the Cloudflare Account ID and an API token with minimum required permissions. The default DNS target supports reverse proxy publishing. The guide never saves credentials.
UserGuide.domain.tabs.title: DNS and reverse proxy share one domain workspace
UserGuide.domain.tabs.text: DNS manages zones and records; Reverse Proxy publishes VM services as URLs. Switching tabs changes no settings.
UserGuide.domain.recordForm.title: Adding a DNS record opens the full form
UserGuide.domain.recordForm.text: Choose A, AAAA, CNAME, or another type, then set name, content, TTL, and proxy behavior. The guide never creates the record.
UserGuide.emptySimulation.title: Run through the complete flow in a simulation
UserGuide.emptySimulation.text: This page currently has no data, so the guide uses an example tailored to the page to demonstrate opening details, switching settings, and using the primary action. Nothing is saved.
